extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners (practitioners, managers, and researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for measuring and interpreting the implementation (outputs) and impact (outcomes) of public relations programs, including metrics, measurement methods, evaluation levels, and how to present and use results for management. Covers attention, knowledge, opinion/attitude/behavior change, repeated behavior, goal/societal impact, and practical measurement techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience reach and frequency (potential exposure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience reach and frequency figures (from firms such as Traffic Audit Bureau for Media Measurement and Simmons Market Research Bureau) estimate exposure to outdoor and transit advertising using local ridership and attendance figures; event/meeting/exhibit attendance figures also measure potential exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These measures indicate potential audience size (who may have been exposed) but do not by themselves indicate program effectiveness—they are implementation/output measures and must be complemented by attention and impact measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting metrics for online and social media (site traffic indicators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Online/social metrics include numbers of users, followers, posts, visits, fans, page views, tab views, likes, interactions, comments, bookmarks, referrals, and other platform-provided counting metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such counts are indicators of potential audience or site traffic and can be 'digital trivia'—useful as measures of attention or implementation but not equivalent to outcomes or program impact. Objectives should specify what these metrics are intended to indicate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attentive audience (attention measurement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of people who actually attend to messages or events—i.e., pay attention—measured by readership, listenership, and viewership studies and equivalent online attention metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attention must be measured because many people pass by signage, skip articles, or have media on without attending. Use readership/listenership/viewership studies and comparable online attention metrics; attention metrics are a distinct evaluation step between exposure and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Starch recognition (aided recall) readership levels: Noted, Associated, Read Most
rubrics_metrics.description: Daniel Starch’s recognition method divides readers into: 'Noted' (recall seeing the ad), 'Associated' (recall and remember advertiser name), and 'Read most' (read ≥50% of copy and recall content). It is an 'aided recall' technique where respondents are shown the material and asked if they recall it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful print-ad readership technique; provides graded evidence of attention and processing of message content. Employ with magazine/newspaper readership data from market research firms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radio/TV audience measurement — Diary method
rubrics_metrics.description: Diary method: household member(s) keep written logs of listening/viewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Has built-in participation bias—those who agree to keep diaries may differ systematically from nonparticipants; be aware of this limitation when interpreting diary-based ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radio/TV audience measurement — Meter method
rubrics_metrics.description: Meter method: electronic meters record set tuning by channel/frequency and time of day, reporting data (e.g., overnight Nielsen ratings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meters record tuning but cannot reliably detect who (if anyone) or how many people are watching or listening, limiting inferences about audience composition or attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radio/TV audience measurement — People meter
rubrics_metrics.description: People meters: each person in a metered home has a button to push when watching so the meter records which person is watching which program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempts to address missing information from audimeters but has issues—respondent fatigue (punching in/out), difficulty for young children, and incomplete metering of all sets in a home leading to incomplete household viewing data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radio/TV audience measurement — Telephone interview (coincidental survey)
rubrics_metrics.description: Telephone interview method: calls made during (coincidental surveys) or after programs to determine audience size and composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increasingly challenged by answering machines, cell phones, caller-ID, and telemarketing fatigue causing nonresponse and sampling biases; interpret telephone-based estimates cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate every step in program implementation (distribution vs. content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment must consider each step in implementation—for example, distribution failures can explain low readership even when content is rated highly (illustrated by employee newsletter case where distribution, not content, was the problem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design evaluation to diagnose where breakdowns occur (preparation, distribution, implementation) rather than assuming content alone determines outcomes; this supports corrective action at the appropriate stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of benchmarks, intermediate (formative) and summative impact assessments
rubrics_metrics.description: Benchmarks (formative research) establish the starting point; intermediate/ interim impact assessments (e.g., media analysis) monitor progress; summative impact assessments provide evidence of success or failure at the planned end point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify criteria for impact in objectives; use summative impact evaluations as input (formative) for the next program cycle; clearly define nature and magnitude of expected changes in knowledge, predisposition, and behavior for each target public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge gain (impact criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the number of people who learn message content—changes in knowledge, awareness, and understanding among target publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the same variables used before the program (pretest) and compare using repeated measures with the same or similar people, or with a comparable control group. Knowledge is often a precursor to interest or action but must be distinguished from attitudes and behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion change (impact criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure how many people change or form opinions about an issue as a result of the program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opinion-change questions differ from knowledge questions; customized indicators (including social media sentiment shifts) should be specified in objectives. Opinion change can occur without knowledge change and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitude change (impact criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attitude change involves altering broad, cross-situational predispositions—more stable than opinions and less subject to short-term change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attitudes typically require longer time and broader measurement across related issues to assess change; do not conflate single-issue opinion shifts with underlying attitude change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior change (impact criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the number of people who act in the desired fashion (actual behavioral change).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess via self-reports (surveys), direct observation (turnstiles, head counts, tallies), and indirect observation (official records, by-products of behavior). Surveys can be unreliable for sensitive behaviors; include validation questions. Combine multiple methods for validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeated behavior (sustained impact criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs aiming for sustained change must measure continued or repeated behavior over time (not one-off actions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow-up measurement over months or years may be required (e.g., smoking cessation, contraception use). Short-term counts immediately after interventions are insufficient to claim sustained behavior change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goal achieved (summative/end-state criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate summative evidence: achievement of program goal such as election results, legislative outcomes, or fund-raising totals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objectives should specify summative criteria. Intermediate outcomes (knowledge, opinion, behavior) may occur without goal attainment; evaluation must extend to goal-level evidence and consider alternative causal explanations for observed changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social and cultural change (ultimate societal impact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of programs’ contribution to broad social and cultural change—long-term, large-scale shifts in norms, institutions, or population health/behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation at this level is confounded by time and multiple causal factors and is usually the domain of scholars; nevertheless, consider societal-level indicators when program theory aims at broad change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for observing and measuring behavior (direct, indirect, unobtrusive, ethnography)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct observation (turnstiles, head counts), indirect records (client appointments, maintenance records, checkout logs), unobtrusive measures (by-products of behavior), and ethnography (participant observation) are methods to measure behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unobtrusive measures do not require cooperation and avoid contaminating behavior but can require ingenuity. Ethnography can be powerful but costly and difficult for clients to understand; choose methods appropriate to the behavior and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data reduction and display (interpreting evaluation results)
rubrics_metrics.description: Raw data from surveys and other measures must be reduced (tabulation, categorization of open-ends) and displayed (tables, charts) to convey main categories, themes and leading statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate conclusions back to original objectives and present results in management-friendly formats (charts/graphs with short headlines). Data reduction and thoughtful display are essential for interpretation and managerial action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting null or unexpected findings (three possible explanations)
rubrics_metrics.description: When expected impact is not detected, possible interpretations are: (1) theory behind strategy was faulty; (2) program preparation/implementation errors occurred; (3) evaluation methods failed to detect the impact (wrong people, invalid/unreliable measures, effect too small).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider these alternatives systematically; check research design, measurement validity, sampling (target vs. general public), and implementation fidelity before concluding program failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations to increase research acceptance and use by management
rubrics_metrics.description: Ten recommendations to increase probability that research is accepted and used by senior management: (1) relate findings to managers’ current concerns; (2) maintain frequent/direct participation with potential users; (3) limit reports to findings with immediate application or clear long-term implications; (4) report only implications logically derived from data; (5) use researchers with established credibility; (6) use rigorous research designs and methods; (7) emphasize corroborating information and minimize negative surprises; (8) enlist sponsorship of key managers; (9) invest time to persuade users to understand and apply findings; (10) conduct research ethically and responsibly respecting human/civil rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow these steps to improve uptake—translate findings into managers’ language, use credible researchers and sound methods, be strategic about what to report, and secure managerial sponsorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate evaluation feedback into planning (feedback loops)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation findings from each stage should be looped back into planning—if pretesting or early feedback shows a medium is inappropriate, practitioners should not proceed to distribute through that medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use formative and interim evaluation results to adjust strategy and tactics before full implementation. Although some models are criticized for not showing explicit feedback, the practice and accompanying literature imply iterative application of findings to planning.
